html:
Java Man is the name for early human fossils found in 1891 and 1892 at Trinil, on the Solo River in East Java. They were the first fossils of the species now called Homo erectus and are between about 700,000 and 1.5 million years old.

The Dutch doctor Eugène Dubois went to the Dutch East Indies as an army surgeon for one purpose: to find the "missing link" between apes and humans that followers of Darwin expected in Asia. His team, working mostly with convict labour, dug up a tooth, a skullcap and a thighbone. The skull was small, but the thigh showed the creature walked upright. He named it Pithecanthropus erectus, "upright ape-man".

At the time it was the oldest human-like fossil ever found, and it caused a storm. Within ten years almost eighty books and articles had been written on it. Some experts said it was an ape, others a modern human, others a side branch with no link to us.

Later finds settled it:

  • Fossils of Peking Man, found near Beijing in the 1920s and 1930s, looked much the same.
  • In 1950 the biologist Ernst Mayr put both into one species, Homo erectus, on the direct line of human evolution.

Java Man remains the type specimen of Homo erectus, the first human species known to have spread out of Africa across Asia. Java has since given up many more fossils, and the island of Flores to the east produced the tiny Homo floresiensis in 2004. Finds in Africa, like Lucy, later pushed the human story much further back.
sum: Java Man is the name for early human fossils found in 1891 and 1892 at Trinil, on the Solo River in East Java. They were the first fossils of the species now called Homo erectus and are between about 700,000 and 1.5 million years old.
